workedExamples.title: When the variable cancels to a TRUE statement: 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12

steps.prompt: Distribute the 4 on the left side. What does 4(x + 3) become?
steps.reveal: 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12. So the equation reads 4x + 12 = 4x + 12. The two sides are already identical.

steps.prompt: Subtract 4x from both sides to gather the variable terms. What is left?
steps.reveal: 4x − 4x = 0 on both sides, leaving 12 = 12. The variable did not vanish to zero — it cancelled because both sides grew at the same rate.

steps.prompt: Is 12 = 12 true or false?
steps.reveal: True. 12 always equals 12, no matter what x is.

steps.prompt: So how many solutions does the equation have? Be careful — does 'the x disappeared' mean x = 0?
steps.reveal: Infinitely many solutions. Every value of x makes the original equation true, because the two sides are the same expression. This is NOT x = 0: x = 0 would be a single answer, but here you never solved for a value at all — you reached a true statement (12 = 12), which means EVERY x works.

workedExamples.title: When the variable cancels to a FALSE statement: 5x + 2 = 5x + 9

steps.prompt: The variable term is the same on both sides (5x). Subtract 5x from both sides. What is left?
steps.reveal: 5x − 5x = 0 on both sides, leaving 2 = 9. The variable terms cancelled because both sides change at the same rate.

steps.prompt: Is 2 = 9 true or false?
steps.reveal: False. 2 never equals 9 — there is nothing left to solve and no leftover equation like 2x = 9 to finish.

steps.prompt: Could you finish by writing x = something, for example x = 9/2 or x = 2?
steps.reveal: No. There is no x term left, so there is nothing to divide — 2 = 9 is a flat contradiction, not a step on the way to a value. Treating it as a solvable leftover is the classic error.

steps.prompt: So how many solutions does the equation have?
steps.reveal: No solution. The statement 2 = 9 is impossible, so no value of x can make the original equation true.

nodes.title: The Coordinate Plane
nodes.objective: Plot and read ordered pairs across all four quadrants.

contextHooks.baseball: A spray chart: x is pull-side to oppo, y is depth.
contextHooks.softball: Plot hit locations: left-right of second base versus distance.

workedExamples.title: Plotting an ordered pair: where does (3, -2) go? (x first, then y)

steps.prompt: An ordered pair is written (x, y). In (3, -2), which number is x and which is y?
steps.reveal: x = 3 (the first number) and y = -2 (the second number). The x-coordinate always comes first. A handy phrase: 'x before y, just like the alphabet.'

steps.prompt: Start at the origin (0, 0). Use the x-coordinate first. Which way and how far do you move for x = 3?
steps.reveal: Move 3 units to the RIGHT along the horizontal x-axis, because 3 is positive. The x-coordinate controls left/right movement only.

steps.prompt: Now use the y-coordinate. From there, which way and how far do you move for y = -2?
steps.reveal: Move 2 units DOWN, because -2 is negative. The y-coordinate controls up/down movement only.

steps.prompt: You moved right 3, then down 2. What point did you land on, and why isn't it (-2, 3)?
steps.reveal: You land on (3, -2): right 3, down 2. If you had moved using -2 first you would have gone left 2 then up 3 and landed on (-2, 3) — a completely different point. Order matters: (3, -2) is not the same as (-2, 3).

workedExamples.title: Which quadrant? Using the signs of (-4, 1)

steps.prompt: The four quadrants are numbered counter-clockwise starting from the top right. What signs (x, y) does each quadrant have?
steps.reveal: Quadrant I: (+, +) top right. Quadrant II: (-, +) top left. Quadrant III: (-, -) bottom left. Quadrant IV: (+, -) bottom right. Only the SIGNS matter for naming the quadrant.

steps.prompt: Look at (-4, 1). What is the sign of the x-coordinate, and what does that tell you about left vs. right?
steps.reveal: x = -4 is negative, so the point is to the LEFT of the y-axis. That narrows it to Quadrant II or Quadrant III.

steps.prompt: Now the y-coordinate: what is the sign of y = 1, and is the point above or below the x-axis?
steps.reveal: y = 1 is positive, so the point is ABOVE the x-axis. Left and above together means the top-left region.

steps.prompt: Combine the signs (-, +). Which quadrant is (-4, 1) in, and what is the classic trap?
steps.reveal: (-, +) is Quadrant II. The classic trap is reading the negative x and jumping to Quadrant III without checking the y-sign — but a positive y means it's above the axis, so it must be Quadrant II, not III.

p1.prompt: A scout plots each at-bat as (game number, hits). In game 4 you got 2 hits. Type that point as (x, y).
hints: The first number is x (game number), the second is y (hits).

p1.prompt: On a hitting chart, your batting-average trend point is at (-3, 5): 3 games below the season midpoint, 5 points above your target average. Which quadrant is (-3, 5) in?

p1.prompt: A pitcher's plot point is (-2, -4): 2 starts below average in innings, 4 below average in strikeouts. Which quadrant is (-2, -4) in?
hints: Both coordinates are negative.

p1.prompt: You chart a runner's path as a point that is 5 to the right of home and 6 below it, written (5, -6). Type the ordered pair as (x, y).

nodes.title: Relations & Functions
nodes.objective: Identify functions as relations assigning exactly one output to each input.

contextHooks.baseball: Each game number maps to exactly one final score — a function.
contextHooks.softball: Jersey number → player is a function; position → player isn't.
contextHooks.basketball: Each minute mark has one score margin; margins repeat, minutes don't.
contextHooks.soccer: Match day → result is a function of the schedule.
contextHooks.football: Each play number produces exactly one yardage outcome.
contextHooks.volleyball: Each rally has one winner — rally number maps to one team.
contextHooks.neutral: A function assigns each input exactly one output.

workedExamples.title: The vertical-line test: does the graph show a function?

steps.prompt: A relation is a function when every input (x-value) is paired with exactly one output (y-value). On a graph, the vertical-line test checks this. What does a vertical line represent?
steps.reveal: A vertical line is the set of all points that share one single x-value. Sliding it left and right lets you check, one input at a time, how many outputs that input has.

steps.prompt: Picture the graph of a sideways parabola opening to the right (like x = y²). Sweep a vertical line across it. At x = 4, how many points does the line touch?
steps.reveal: Two points: (4, 2) and (4, −2). The single input x = 4 is paired with two outputs, 2 and −2.

steps.prompt: State the rule for the vertical-line test based on what you just saw.
steps.reveal: If ANY vertical line crosses the graph more than once, the relation is NOT a function. If every possible vertical line hits the graph at most once, it IS a function.

steps.prompt: So is the sideways parabola a function? And what is the common reading mistake?
steps.reveal: It is NOT a function, because the vertical line at x = 4 hits twice. The classic mistake is reading the test horizontally or only checking a spot where the line happens to hit once — you must be able to find even one vertical line that hits twice to disqualify it.

steps.prompt: Now consider an upward parabola, y = x². Apply the same sweep. Function or not?
steps.reveal: Every vertical line hits y = x² exactly once, so it IS a function. Many inputs (like x = 2 and x = −2) share the output 4 — that is allowed. A function only forbids one input giving two outputs, never two inputs sharing one output.

workedExamples.title: Function vs. one-to-one: don't conflate them

steps.prompt: Look at the relation {(1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 9)}. Is each input paired with exactly one output?
steps.reveal: Yes. Input 1 → 5, input 2 → 5, input 3 → 9. Every input has exactly one output, so this IS a function.

steps.prompt: Inputs 1 and 2 both map to output 5. Does that break the function rule?
steps.reveal: No. The function rule only restricts OUTPUTS per input — each input may have just one output. Two different inputs sharing the same output is completely allowed. This is called many-to-one.

steps.prompt: A function is one-to-one when, in addition to being a function, every output also comes from exactly one input. Is {(1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 9)} one-to-one?
steps.reveal: No. The output 5 is produced by two inputs, 1 and 2. So it is a function but NOT one-to-one.

steps.prompt: Now test {(1, 5), (2, 7), (3, 9)}. Function? One-to-one?
steps.reveal: Function: yes, each input has one output. One-to-one: yes, each output (5, 7, 9) traces back to exactly one input. So this is a function AND one-to-one.

steps.prompt: Why is it wrong to call {(1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 9)} 'not a function'?
steps.reveal: Calling it 'not a function' confuses the one-to-one condition with the function condition. Repeated OUTPUTS never disqualify a function; only a repeated INPUT with differing outputs does. Many-to-one relations are valid functions — they just are not one-to-one.

hints: Ask: does each input (jersey number) point to exactly one output (player)?
One number, one player — that is exactly one output per input.

Two slots sharing the same player is a repeated OUTPUT, which is allowed.

hints: Each player (input) has exactly one total, so it is a function.

workedExamples.title: Evaluate f(x)=mx+b: f(3) means input 3, not f times 3

steps.prompt: A function is defined as f(x) = 2x + 5. You are asked to find f(3). First, what does the 3 inside f(3) tell you to do?
steps.reveal: The 3 is the INPUT. f(3) means "replace every x with 3," not "multiply f by 3." The letter f is the name of the function, not a number you can multiply.

steps.prompt: Rewrite f(x) = 2x + 5 with 3 substituted in place of x.
steps.reveal: f(3) = 2(3) + 5. Notice the x became 3 everywhere it appeared. We did NOT write f · 3.

steps.prompt: Now do the arithmetic: compute 2(3) + 5.
steps.reveal: 2 times 3 is 6, and 6 + 5 = 11. So f(3) = 11.

steps.prompt: Why is the wrong answer 3 (just the input) or 6 (2 times 3 alone) not correct here?
steps.reveal: 3 is only the input you plugged in, and 6 forgets the + 5. The full output is f(3) = 11. The output is the whole expression evaluated, not a piece of it.

workedExamples.title: Solve f(x)=value: which side does the number plug into?

steps.prompt: A function is defined as f(x) = 4x − 1. You are asked: for what input x is f(x) = 19? Before solving, where does the 19 belong?
steps.reveal: f(x) = 19 means the OUTPUT is 19. The 19 replaces the whole expression 4x − 1, not the x. So you set 4x − 1 = 19 and solve for the input x.

steps.prompt: Write the equation you must solve.
steps.reveal: 4x − 1 = 19. The 19 goes on the output side; x stays unknown. A common mistake is plugging 19 in for x — that answers a different question (it finds f(19), not the x that gives 19).

steps.prompt: Solve 4x − 1 = 19 for x. Add 1 to both sides first.
Now divide both sides by 4 to finish.

nodes.title: Domain & Range
nodes.objective: Determine reasonable domains and ranges from graphs, tables, and contexts.

contextHooks.baseball: Innings 1–9 is the domain; runs scored is the range.
contextHooks.softball: Pitch count can't be negative — context restricts the domain.
contextHooks.basketball: Minutes played live in [0, 48]; points form the range.
contextHooks.soccer: Match minutes 0–90 bound the domain of a fitness curve.
contextHooks.football: Down number is a domain of {1, 2, 3, 4} — discrete and finite.
contextHooks.volleyball: Set scores cap the range; rallies index the domain.
contextHooks.neutral: Domain: allowed inputs. Range: resulting outputs.

workedExamples.title: Reading domain (inputs/x) and range (outputs/y) from a table

steps.prompt: A table lists points (x, y): (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7), (4, 9). Which column holds the INPUTS, and what do we call the set of all inputs?
steps.reveal: The x-column holds the inputs. The set of all inputs is the DOMAIN. Inputs go IN — read the x-values: 1, 2, 3, 4.

steps.prompt: Which column holds the OUTPUTS, and what do we call the set of all outputs?
steps.reveal: The y-column holds the outputs. The set of all outputs is the RANGE. Read the y-values: 3, 5, 7, 9.

steps.prompt: Write the domain as a set.
steps.reveal: Domain = {1, 2, 3, 4}. List the x-values, smallest to largest, with no repeats.

steps.prompt: Write the range as a set.
steps.reveal: Range = {3, 5, 7, 9}. These are the y-values. Notice domain and range are DIFFERENT sets — do not swap them.

steps.prompt: A classmate writes Domain = {3, 5, 7, 9}, Range = {1, 2, 3, 4}. What mistake did they make?
steps.reveal: They swapped domain and range. Domain is always the x-values (inputs); range is always the y-values (outputs). Say it out loud: 'x is domain, y is range' to keep them straight.

workedExamples.title: Using a context restriction to find a reasonable domain

steps.prompt: A booster club sells tickets for $8 each. Total money collected is y = 8x, where x is the number of tickets sold. Mathematically, what x-values does y = 8x allow?
steps.reveal: As a bare equation, x could be any real number — negatives, fractions, anything. But this is a CONTEXT, so we must check what x can really mean here.

steps.prompt: What does x stand for, and can it be negative?
steps.reveal: x is the number of tickets sold. You cannot sell a negative number of tickets, so x cannot be below 0. The smallest possible value is 0 (no tickets sold).

steps.prompt: Can x be a fraction, like 2.5 tickets?
steps.reveal: No. You sell whole tickets only, so x must be a whole number: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. Fractions are not allowed by the context.

steps.prompt: State a reasonable domain for this situation.
steps.reveal: Reasonable domain = whole numbers x ≥ 0, that is {0, 1, 2, 3, ...}. The context RESTRICTS the domain — it is not all real numbers.

steps.prompt: Why would 'all real numbers' or 'x can be −5 or 2.5' be wrong answers here?
steps.reveal: Those ignore the context restriction. The math equation allows them, but selling −5 tickets or 2.5 tickets is impossible. Always let the real-world meaning trim the domain to values that make sense.

nodes.title: Slope as Rate of Change
nodes.objective: Interpret slope as a constant rate: change in output per unit input.

contextHooks.baseball: 6 hits by game 4, 18 by game 10 — the line climbs 2 per game.
contextHooks.softball: Strikeouts rising 3 per game traces a steady slope.
contextHooks.basketball: A scorer adding 18 a night has a season line of slope 18.
contextHooks.soccer: Two points per match on average is the table-climb rate.
contextHooks.football: Cumulative yards growing 110 per game — that's the slope.
contextHooks.volleyball: Kills accumulating 4 per set set the line's steepness.
contextHooks.neutral: Slope = rise/run = Δy/Δx, a constant rate.

workedExamples.title: Finding a rate from a table: distance per hour

steps.prompt: A car's odometer reads 120 miles at hour 2 and 300 miles at hour 5. We want the rate in miles per hour. First, what is the change in output (miles)?
steps.reveal: Change in output = 300 − 120 = 180 miles. The output is what we are measuring (miles); its change is the top of the rate, the numerator.

steps.prompt: Now the change in input (hours). What is it?
steps.reveal: Change in input = 5 − 2 = 3 hours. The input is what drives the change (time); its change is the bottom of the rate, the denominator.

steps.prompt: A rate is change in output PER UNIT of input. We have 180 miles for 3 hours — but 'per unit' means per ONE hour. What must we do?
steps.reveal: Divide by the input change to get the amount per single hour: 180 ÷ 3. Do NOT stop at 180 — 180 is the total change, not the rate. Forgetting to divide by the denominator is the most common error here.

steps.prompt: Compute the rate.
steps.reveal: 180 ÷ 3 = 60. The slope is 60 miles per hour: for every 1 additional hour, distance grows by 60 miles.

steps.prompt: Check: does 60 mph match the table?
steps.reveal: From hour 2 to hour 5 is 3 hours; 3 × 60 = 180 miles gained, and 120 + 180 = 300. It matches. The rate is the constant 60 miles per 1 hour — always per UNIT input.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting slope in words: units and rise/run vs run/rise

steps.prompt: A plant grows so that its height rises 6 cm every 2 weeks. Write this as a rate change in output per unit input.
steps.reveal: Output is height (cm), input is time (weeks). Rate = 6 cm ÷ 2 weeks = 3. The slope is 3 cm per week.

steps.prompt: Slope is rise over run: rise/run = Δoutput/Δinput. Which quantity is the rise and which is the run here?
steps.reveal: Rise = Δoutput = 6 cm (the vertical change, height). Run = Δinput = 2 weeks (the horizontal change, time). Slope = rise/run = 6/2 = 3 cm per week.

steps.prompt: A classmate writes the rate as 2/6 = 1/3, 'a third of a week per cm.' What did they do wrong?
steps.reveal: They computed run/rise (input over output) instead of rise/run (output over input). That is the inverted ratio — it is the reciprocal and answers a different question. Slope must be output per input cm per week, not week per cm.

steps.prompt: State the slope's meaning in a full sentence with correct units.
steps.reveal: The slope of 3 means the height increases by 3 cm for each 1 additional week. Pattern: '(output units) per 1 (input unit)' — here, 3 centimeters per week.

steps.prompt: Why does the order rise/run matter so much?
steps.reveal: Because rise/run and run/rise are reciprocals: 3 cm per week is very different from 1/3 week per cm. The question 'how fast does height change per week?' fixes output on top, input on bottom. Naming the units forces the correct order.

nodes.title: Slope from Two Points
nodes.objective: Compute slope from coordinate pairs using m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

workedExamples.title: Slope from two points with m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)

steps.prompt: You are given two points, (2, 3) and (6, 11). To find the slope, label them: which numbers are x₁, y₁, x₂, y₂?
steps.reveal: Take (2, 3) as point 1, so x₁ = 2 and y₁ = 3. Take (6, 11) as point 2, so x₂ = 6 and y₂ = 11. The labels are your choice, but once you pick them you must use them consistently.

steps.prompt: Write the slope formula and substitute the labeled values.
steps.reveal: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (11 − 3)/(6 − 2). The top is the change in y; the bottom is the change in x.

steps.prompt: Compute the numerator (the rise) and the denominator (the run).
steps.reveal: Numerator: 11 − 3 = 8. Denominator: 6 − 2 = 4. Slope is rise over run, so you still need to divide — the 8 alone is NOT the slope.

steps.prompt: Divide to find the slope.
steps.reveal: m = 8 / 4 = 2. The line rises 2 units for every 1 unit it moves right. Stopping at the rise of 8 and forgetting to divide by the run is the most common error here.

workedExamples.title: Subtraction order must match in the top and bottom

steps.prompt: Use the points (1, 2) and (4, 8). First compute the slope taking (1, 2) as point 1 and (4, 8) as point 2.
steps.reveal: m = (8 − 2)/(4 − 1) = 6/3 = 2. The line has slope 2.

steps.prompt: Now reverse which point is first: take (4, 8) as point 1 and (1, 2) as point 2. Compute the slope again.
steps.reveal: m = (2 − 8)/(1 − 4) = (−6)/(−3) = 2. Same slope. As long as the top and bottom are subtracted in the SAME order, the order you pick does not matter.

steps.prompt: Here is the trap. What happens if you subtract y in one order but x in the other: (8 − 2)/(1 − 4)?
steps.reveal: That gives 6/(−3) = −2. The sign is now wrong. Mixing the subtraction order — y₂ − y₁ on top but x₁ − x₂ on the bottom — flips the slope's sign.

steps.prompt: State the rule that keeps you safe.
steps.reveal: Subtract the coordinates in the same order in both the numerator and the denominator. If y₂ comes first on top, then x₂ must come first on the bottom. This inconsistent-subtraction-order mistake turns a +2 slope into −2.

nodes.title: Patterns, Tables & Graphs
nodes.objective: Move between tables, rules, and graphs of linear patterns.

contextHooks.baseball: A hits-by-game table becomes a rule, then a line.
contextHooks.softball: Inning-by-inning K table → expression → graph.
contextHooks.basketball: Quarter scores tabled, ruled, and graphed as one pattern.
contextHooks.soccer: Matchday points table converts to a climbing line.
contextHooks.football: Drive-by-drive yardage table reveals the per-drive rule.
contextHooks.volleyball: Set-by-set kill table maps to a straight-line trend.
contextHooks.neutral: Same linear relationship, three representations.

workedExamples.title: Deriving the rule y = mx + b from a table (a row is a point, not the rule)

steps.prompt: This table shows x = 1,2,3,4 with y = 5,8,11,14. The y-values rise as x rises. To find the rule, first find how much y changes each time x goes up by 1. What is that constant difference?
steps.reveal: From 5 to 8 is +3, from 8 to 11 is +3, from 11 to 14 is +3. The constant difference is 3. Because it is the same every step, this is a linear pattern and m = 3.

steps.prompt: Some students grab the row (1, 5) and announce the rule is 'y = 5x' because 5 is sitting right there. Why is that wrong?
steps.reveal: A single row is just one point on the line, not the rule. Testing y = 5x at x = 2 gives 10, but the table says 8. One row never gives you the slope by itself — you must compare how y changes across rows.

steps.prompt: You have m = 3. Now find b, the value of y when x = 0. The table starts at x = 1 where y = 5. Step backward one x to x = 0.
steps.reveal: Going from x = 1 back to x = 0 means y drops by the constant difference 3: 5 − 3 = 2. So when x = 0, y = 2. That means b = 2.

steps.prompt: Write the rule using m = 3 and b = 2, then check it against a row you did NOT use to find b.
steps.reveal: The rule is y = 3x + 2. Check x = 4: 3(4) + 2 = 14, which matches the table. The rule works for every row — that is what makes it the rule, not any single row.

workedExamples.title: Plotting a table on a graph: each row is the point (x, y) in that order

steps.prompt: This table has x = 0,1,2,3 and y = 1,4,7,10. To graph it, you turn each row into a point. Take the first row: x = 0, y = 1. Write it as an ordered pair.
steps.reveal: The row becomes the point (0, 1). The x-value always goes first, the y-value second: (x, y). Here that is (0, 1).

steps.prompt: Plot (0, 1). Which direction is the x-coordinate, and which is the y-coordinate?
steps.reveal: Start at the origin. The first number, 0, is horizontal (left-right), so you do not move sideways. The second number, 1, is vertical (up-down), so you move up 1. The point sits on the y-axis at height 1.

steps.prompt: Here is the classic trap. The next row is x = 1, y = 4. A student plots it as (4, 1) — moving 4 right and 1 up. Is that the same point as (1, 4)?
steps.reveal: No. (1, 4) means 1 right and 4 up; (4, 1) means 4 right and 1 up. They are different locations. Swapping the pair plots the wrong point. The row x = 1, y = 4 must be plotted as (1, 4), x first.

steps.prompt: Plot the remaining rows as ordered pairs and describe what the four points form.
steps.reveal: The points are (0, 1), (1, 4), (2, 7), (3, 10). Each x goes up 1 while each y goes up 3, so the points line up straight — a line with slope 3 crossing the y-axis at 1. Plotting any pair reversed would knock that point off the line.

contextHooks.baseball: y = 2x + 7: 7 hits banked, 2 added per game.
contextHooks.softball: Starting 3 K with 3 more per inning: y = 3x + 3.

workedExamples.title: Reading slope and y-intercept from y = mx + b

steps.prompt: Look at y = 3x + 5. In the form y = mx + b, the letter m is the slope and b is the y-intercept. Which number is multiplied by x?
steps.reveal: The 3 is multiplied by x. The number multiplied by x is the COEFFICIENT of x, and that coefficient is always the slope m.

steps.prompt: So what is the slope of y = 3x + 5?
steps.reveal: The slope is m = 3. Slope is the coefficient of x — never the lonely constant on the end.

steps.prompt: Now find b. Which number stands alone, with no x attached?
steps.reveal: The 5 stands alone. The constant with no x is b, the y-intercept. So b = 5.

steps.prompt: A classmate says the slope is 5 and the y-intercept is 3. What did they do wrong?
steps.reveal: They swapped m and b. The slope must be the coefficient of x (3) and the y-intercept must be the constant (5). Always match m to the x-term and b to the constant — do not trade their places.

steps.prompt: State the slope and the y-intercept of y = 3x + 5.
steps.reveal: Slope m = 3, y-intercept b = 5. The coefficient of x is the slope; the constant is the y-intercept.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting b as the starting value when x = 0

steps.prompt: A line is y = 2x + 4. We want to interpret b = 4. What is y when x = 0? Substitute 0 for x.
steps.reveal: y = 2(0) + 4 = 0 + 4 = 4. When x = 0, y equals b. So at x = 0, y = 4.

steps.prompt: The point where x = 0 sits on which axis?
steps.reveal: On the y-axis. Every point with x = 0 lies on the y-axis, so b tells you where the line crosses the y-axis.

steps.prompt: Write the y-intercept of y = 2x + 4 as a point (x, y).
steps.reveal: It is the point (0, 4). The y-intercept is a POINT on the y-axis with x = 0 and y = b — it is a y-value, not an x-value.

steps.prompt: In y = 2x + 4 modeling a savings plan where x is weeks, what does b = 4 mean?
steps.reveal: b = 4 is the starting amount: the value of y before any weeks pass, when x = 0. It is the beginning balance, $4.

steps.prompt: A classmate marks the y-intercept at (4, 0) on the x-axis. Why is that wrong?
steps.reveal: They treated b as an x-value. The y-intercept is (0, 4), on the y-axis — b is the y-value when x = 0, not a spot along the x-axis.

nodes.title: Graphing Linear Equations
nodes.objective: Graph a line from slope-intercept form using the intercept and rise/run.

contextHooks.baseball: Plot the 7-hit start, climb 2-per-game, draw the pace line.
contextHooks.softball: Graph the strikeout pace and read the record-breaking game.
contextHooks.basketball: Draw the 18-a-night line and project game 30.
contextHooks.soccer: The points line shows exactly when 40 points arrives.

workedExamples.title: Plot the y-intercept on the y-axis, then use rise/run

steps.prompt: You are given y = 2x + 3. In slope-intercept form y = mx + b, identify the slope m and the y-intercept b.
steps.reveal: Here m = 2 and b = 3. The slope is 2 (think of it as the fraction 2/1, rise 2 over run 1). The y-intercept is 3.

steps.prompt: Plot the y-intercept. Which point does b = 3 give you, and on which axis does it sit?
steps.reveal: The y-intercept is ALWAYS the point (0, b) = (0, 3). It sits on the y-axis, where x = 0. A common mistake is plotting it at (3, 0) on the x-axis — that is wrong. b lives on the y-axis.

steps.prompt: From the starting point (0, 3), use the slope as rise/run = 2/1. Which way do you move?
steps.reveal: Run 1 to the right (x increases by 1) and rise 2 up (y increases by 2). Because the slope is positive, the rise is upward.

steps.prompt: Where does that rise/run step land the second point?
steps.reveal: Start at (0, 3); move right 1 to x = 1 and up 2 to y = 3 + 2 = 5. The second point is (1, 5). Draw the line through (0, 3) and (1, 5).

workedExamples.title: A negative slope means the rise goes DOWN

steps.prompt: You are given y = −3x + 4. Identify the slope m and the y-intercept b.
steps.reveal: Here m = −3 and b = 4. As a fraction the slope is −3/1: a rise of −3 over a run of 1.

steps.prompt: Plot the y-intercept. What point is it, and on which axis?
steps.reveal: The y-intercept is (0, b) = (0, 4), on the y-axis where x = 0. Not (4, 0) — that would be on the x-axis.

steps.prompt: The slope is −3/1. From (0, 4), run 1 to the right. Because the slope is negative, do you go up or down?
steps.reveal: DOWN. A negative slope falls as you move right. Run 1 right, then rise −3 means move 3 DOWN. Moving up 3 instead would be the direction error to avoid.

steps.prompt: Where does the correct step land the second point?
steps.reveal: Start at (0, 4); move right 1 to x = 1 and down 3 to y = 4 − 3 = 1. The second point is (1, 1). If you had wrongly gone up, you would land at (1, 7) — that is the direction error.

nodes.title: x- and y-Intercepts
nodes.objective: Find and interpret intercepts from equations and graphs.

contextHooks.baseball: The y-intercept is hits before game one; x-intercept, when a deficit clears.
contextHooks.softball: Where the run-differential line crosses zero is the comeback game.
contextHooks.basketball: A point-margin line's x-intercept is the tie moment.
contextHooks.soccer: Goal differential hitting zero marks level on aggregate.
contextHooks.football: x-intercept: the drive where negative field position is erased.
contextHooks.volleyball: A deficit line crossing zero is when the set draws even.
contextHooks.neutral: x-intercept: set y = 0. y-intercept: set x = 0.

workedExamples.title: Finding both intercepts of 3x + 2y = 12: which variable do you set to zero?

steps.prompt: To find the x-intercept, the graph is crossing the x-axis. On the x-axis, what is the value of y?
steps.reveal: On the x-axis, y = 0. The x-axis is the horizontal line where height is zero, so every point on it has y = 0. That is the variable you set to zero to find the x-intercept — NOT x.

steps.prompt: Set y = 0 in 3x + 2y = 12 and solve for x.
steps.reveal: 3x + 2(0) = 12 becomes 3x = 12, so x = 4. The x-intercept value is 4.

steps.prompt: Now the y-intercept: the graph is crossing the y-axis. On the y-axis, what is the value of x?
steps.reveal: On the y-axis, x = 0. The classic swap error is setting y = 0 again — but for the y-intercept you zero the OTHER variable, x.

steps.prompt: Set x = 0 in 3x + 2y = 12 and solve for y.
steps.reveal: 3(0) + 2y = 12 becomes 2y = 12, so y = 6. The y-intercept value is 6.

steps.prompt: State the rule that keeps you from swapping.
steps.reveal: For the x-intercept, set y = 0 (you want where it touches the x-axis, where height is 0). For the y-intercept, set x = 0. You always zero the OTHER variable from the one named in the intercept.

workedExamples.title: Intercepts are POINTS: writing (a, 0) and (0, b) for y = 2x - 8

steps.prompt: Find the x-intercept value of y = 2x - 8 by setting y = 0.
steps.reveal: 0 = 2x - 8, so 2x = 8 and x = 4. The x-intercept value is 4.

steps.prompt: An intercept is a location on the graph, not just one number. Write the x-intercept as an ordered pair (x, y).
steps.reveal: The x-intercept is the point (4, 0). The y-coordinate is 0 because the x-intercept sits ON the x-axis. Writing just '4' or writing (0, 4) loses where the point actually is.

steps.prompt: Find the y-intercept value by setting x = 0.
steps.reveal: y = 2(0) - 8 = -8. The y-intercept value is -8.

steps.prompt: Write the y-intercept as an ordered pair (x, y).
steps.reveal: The y-intercept is the point (0, -8). The x-coordinate is 0 because it sits ON the y-axis. The zero goes in the FIRST slot for a y-intercept and the SECOND slot for an x-intercept.

steps.prompt: Are (4, 0) and (0, -8) the same point?
steps.reveal: No — they are two different points in different places. (4, 0) is on the x-axis, (0, -8) is on the y-axis. They are the two spots where the single line crosses the two axes. The zero is never in the same slot for both.

workedExamples.title: Substituting a point and slope into point-slope form: slope 4 through (−3, 2)

steps.prompt: Point-slope form is y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Identify m, x₁, and y₁ for slope 4 through the point (−3, 2).
steps.reveal: The slope is m = 4. The point gives x₁ = −3 and y₁ = 2. Order matters: the first coordinate is x₁, the second is y₁.

steps.prompt: Substitute m = 4 and y₁ = 2 first. What does the left side and the front of the right side look like?
steps.reveal: y − y₁ becomes y − 2, and m becomes 4, so far: y − 2 = 4(x − x₁). Now only x₁ is left to plug in.

steps.prompt: Now substitute x₁ = −3 into (x − x₁). Watch the sign: you are subtracting a NEGATIVE.
steps.reveal: x − x₁ = x − (−3). Subtracting −3 is the same as adding 3, so x − (−3) = x + 3. The double negative turns into a plus.

steps.prompt: Write the finished equation.
steps.reveal: y − 2 = 4(x + 3). The classic trap is writing y − 2 = 4(x − 3), which loses the sign flip. Because x₁ = −3, the inside must read x + 3, not x − 3.

workedExamples.title: Converting point-slope to slope-intercept: distribute to BOTH terms

steps.prompt: Start from y − 5 = 3(x − 2). To reach slope-intercept form y = mx + b, what is the first move?
steps.reveal: Distribute the 3 across the parentheses. You must multiply EVERY term inside (x − 2) by 3 — both the x and the −2.

steps.prompt: Multiply 3 by the first term, x. What do you get?
steps.reveal: 3 · x = 3x. This is the part everyone remembers.

steps.prompt: Now multiply 3 by the SECOND term, −2. Do not stop after the first term.
steps.reveal: 3 · (−2) = −6. So the right side becomes 3x − 6. Forgetting this second product is the partial-distribution trap: it would leave you with the wrong 3x − 2.

steps.prompt: You now have y − 5 = 3x − 6. Isolate y by adding 5 to both sides.
steps.reveal: y = 3x − 6 + 5 = 3x − 1. So b = −1. Had you distributed to only the first term (y − 5 = 3x − 2), you would have gotten b = 3 — wrong.

workedExamples.title: Solving standard form for y: 4x + 2y = 12

steps.prompt: We have 4x + 2y = 12 in standard form. To reach y = mx + b, we want y alone. What is the first move?
steps.reveal: Get the y-term by itself first. Subtract 4x from BOTH sides: 2y = -4x + 12. Notice the 4x became NEGATIVE when it crossed the equals sign.

steps.prompt: Why did +4x turn into -4x?
steps.reveal: Moving a term across the equals sign reverses its sign, because you are subtracting it from both sides. The most common error here is leaving it positive and writing 2y = 4x + 12. Keep the minus sign.

steps.prompt: Now we have 2y = -4x + 12. How do we get a single y?
steps.reveal: Divide EVERY term by 2: y = (-4x)/2 + 12/2, which gives y = -2x + 6.

steps.prompt: What is the slope, and what is the sign trap to avoid?
steps.reveal: The slope is -2 (negative). The trap is answering +2 by forgetting the sign when 4x crossed over. Slope = -A/B = -4/2 = -2. The y-intercept is 6.

steps.prompt: Final check: rewrite the result and confirm it matches.
steps.reveal: y = -2x + 6. Slope -2, y-intercept 6. Substituting x = 0 gives y = 6, and the original 4(0) + 2(6) = 12 checks out.

workedExamples.title: Graphing standard form by intercepts: 3x + 5y = 30

steps.prompt: We want to graph 3x + 5y = 30 fast using its two intercepts. To find the x-intercept, what do we set to zero?
steps.reveal: Set y = 0, because every point on the x-axis has y = 0. Then 3x + 5(0) = 30, so 3x = 30.

steps.prompt: Solve 3x = 30 for the x-intercept.
steps.reveal: x = 30/3 = 10. The x-intercept is the point (10, 0). Notice x-intercept = C/A = 30/3.

steps.prompt: Now the y-intercept. What do we set to zero this time?
steps.reveal: Set x = 0, because every point on the y-axis has x = 0. Then 3(0) + 5y = 30, so 5y = 30.

steps.prompt: Solve 5y = 30 for the y-intercept.
steps.reveal: y = 30/5 = 6. The y-intercept is the point (0, 6). Notice y-intercept = C/B = 30/5.

steps.prompt: What is the shortcut, and what is the trap?
steps.reveal: x-intercept = C/A = 30/3 = 10; y-intercept = C/B = 30/5 = 6. The trap is mixing them up — dividing by the wrong coefficient (using C/B = 6 when the x-intercept was asked). Match A with x, B with y. Plot (10, 0) and (0, 6) and draw the line.

nodes.title: Writing Linear Equations
nodes.objective: Construct linear equations from a slope and point, two points, or a context.

contextHooks.baseball: Two box-score snapshots — write the full season pace equation.
contextHooks.softball: Rate plus one game's total: solve for b, state the model.
contextHooks.basketball: Totals of 60 points after game 3 and 150 after game 8: m = 90/5 = 18, then b = 6 — y = 18x + 6.
contextHooks.soccer: Two table checkpoints define the club's points equation.

contextHooks.neutral: Find m, substitute a point, solve for b, write y = mx + b.

workedExamples.title: Build y = mx + b from a slope and one point: m = 3, point (2, 10)

steps.prompt: We know the slope m = 3 and the line passes through (2, 10). We want y = mx + b. We already have m. What single unknown is left?
steps.reveal: Only b is unknown. The slope slot is filled: y = 3x + b. Now we need the number b that makes the line actually pass through (2, 10).

steps.prompt: A common shortcut error is to just write b = 10 because the point's y is 10. Why is that wrong here?
steps.reveal: b is the y-value only when x = 0. Our point has x = 2, NOT 0, so 10 is the height at x = 2, not the height at x = 0. We must solve for b, not copy the point's y.

steps.prompt: Substitute the point into y = 3x + b. Replace x with 2 and y with 10. What equation do you get?
steps.reveal: 10 = 3(2) + b, which is 10 = 6 + b. Keep x with its matching y: x = 2 goes in the mx slot, y = 10 goes on the left.

steps.prompt: Solve 10 = 6 + b for b.
steps.reveal: Subtract 6 from both sides: b = 10 − 6 = 4. So b = 4, which is NOT the point's y of 10.

steps.prompt: Write the final equation and check it against the point.
steps.reveal: y = 3x + 4. Check: at x = 2, y = 3(2) + 4 = 10. It passes through (2, 10). Final answer: y = 3x + 4.

workedExamples.title: Build y = mx + b from two points: (1, 5) and (3, 11)

steps.prompt: We have two points, (1, 5) and (3, 11), and want y = mx + b. With two points we cannot read m directly, so what do we compute first?
steps.reveal: Find the slope first: m = (change in y)/(change in x) = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1). Slope before intercept.

steps.prompt: Compute the slope. Keep each point's x paired with its OWN y — do not cross a y from one point with an x from the other.
steps.reveal: m = (11 − 5)/(3 − 1) = 6/2 = 3. Notice 11 and 3 come from the SAME point, and 5 and 1 come from the SAME point. Mixing them (like (11 − 5)/(1 − 3)) flips the sign and gives a wrong slope.

steps.prompt: Now use one point to find b. Substitute (1, 5) into y = 3x + b. What equation appears?
steps.reveal: 5 = 3(1) + b, which is 5 = 3 + b. We chose the point (1, 5): x = 1 and y = 5 stay together.

steps.prompt: Solve 5 = 3 + b for b.
steps.reveal: Subtract 3 from both sides: b = 5 − 3 = 2. So b = 2 — again NOT the point's y of 5.

steps.prompt: Write the final equation and verify with the OTHER point (3, 11).
steps.reveal: y = 3x + 2. Check the second point: at x = 3, y = 3(3) + 2 = 11. It passes through (3, 11). Final answer: y = 3x + 2.

nodes.title: Parallel & Perpendicular Lines
nodes.objective: Use slope relationships to identify and write parallel and perpendicular lines.

contextHooks.baseball: Two hitters on identical paces: parallel lines, never crossing.

workedExamples.title: Parallel lines have EQUAL slopes (a different y-intercept does NOT break parallelism)

steps.prompt: Look at the two lines y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x + 8. What is the slope of each line?
steps.reveal: Both have slope 3 — the number multiplying x. Line one rises 3 for every 1 across; line two rises 3 for every 1 across as well.

steps.prompt: The y-intercepts are different (+1 versus +8). A classmate says that because the +1 and +8 differ, the lines cannot be parallel. Is that right?
steps.reveal: No. The y-intercept only decides WHERE a line crosses the y-axis, not its steepness. Parallel is about steepness — that is the slope — not about the intercept.

steps.prompt: What is the rule for two lines to be parallel?
steps.reveal: Two non-vertical lines are parallel exactly when their slopes are EQUAL. The intercepts can be anything; in fact they MUST differ, or the two lines would be the same line.

steps.prompt: So are y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x + 8 parallel?
steps.reveal: Yes. Equal slopes (3 = 3) means parallel. The different intercepts (+1 and +8) just shift one line above the other; they run side by side forever and never meet.

steps.prompt: If you wanted ANY line parallel to y = 3x + 8, what slope must it have?
steps.reveal: Slope 3 — the same slope. For example y = 3x − 5 is parallel to y = 3x + 8. Same slope = parallel, regardless of the y-intercept.

workedExamples.title: Perpendicular slopes are NEGATIVE RECIPROCALS (flip AND change sign)

steps.prompt: A line has slope 2/3. To find a perpendicular slope you do two things: flip the fraction and change the sign. First, flip 2/3. What do you get?
steps.reveal: Flipping (taking the reciprocal of) 2/3 gives 3/2. You swap the numerator and denominator.

steps.prompt: Second step: change the sign. The original slope 2/3 is positive, so what sign does the perpendicular slope take?
steps.reveal: It becomes negative. A positive slope has a negative perpendicular slope, and a negative slope has a positive one. So 3/2 becomes −3/2.

steps.prompt: Putting both steps together, what is the slope perpendicular to 2/3?
steps.reveal: −3/2. This is the NEGATIVE RECIPROCAL of 2/3: reciprocal (flip) gives 3/2, negative (sign change) gives −3/2. Both steps are required.

steps.prompt: Why is doing only ONE step wrong? What if you only changed the sign and got −2/3, or only flipped and got 3/2?
steps.reveal: Neither is perpendicular. Only changing the sign (−2/3) keeps the same steepness, just mirrored — that is the classic negative-reciprocal-error. Only flipping (3/2) keeps it positive and pointing the wrong way. You must do BOTH: flip and change sign.

steps.prompt: Check it: multiply the two slopes 2/3 and −3/2. What do you get, and what does that confirm?
steps.reveal: (2/3)(−3/2) = −6/6 = −1. Perpendicular slopes always multiply to −1. The product being −1 confirms −3/2 is correct.

nodes.title: Graphing Linear Inequalities
nodes.objective: Graph two-variable linear inequalities with correct boundary and shading.

contextHooks.baseball: Pitch-count safety region: combinations under the workload line.

contextHooks.basketball: Minutes restrictions: the allowed (games, minutes) half-plane.

contextHooks.football: Practice-rep limits define a feasible shaded region.

contextHooks.neutral: y > 2x + 1: dashed boundary, shade where the test point works.

workedExamples.title: Boundary style: dashed for strict, solid for 'or equal to'

steps.prompt: We want to graph y > 2x + 1. First, what line do we draw as the boundary?
steps.reveal: Draw the boundary line y = 2x + 1 (replace the inequality sign with =). This line separates the plane into two regions.

steps.prompt: The symbol is > (strictly greater than). Should the boundary line be solid or dashed?
steps.reveal: DASHED. With strict < or >, points exactly ON the line are NOT solutions, so we draw a dashed line to show the line itself is excluded.

steps.prompt: Now compare: graph y >= 2x + 1 instead. Should THIS boundary be solid or dashed?
steps.reveal: SOLID. With <= or >=, points ON the line ARE solutions (equality is allowed), so we draw a solid line to include it.

steps.prompt: State the rule in one sentence so you never mix them up.
steps.reveal: Dashed = the line is NOT included (strict < or >). Solid = the line IS included (<= or >=). The shading comes later; this step only decides the boundary style.

steps.prompt: Quick check: for y < x - 4, is the boundary solid or dashed?
steps.reveal: Dashed, because < is strict. The most common error is drawing it solid out of habit — always look at the symbol first: an underline under the inequality means solid.

workedExamples.title: Test point: substitute (0,0) and shade the TRUE side

steps.prompt: We are shading y > 2x + 1 (boundary already drawn dashed). To decide which side to shade, we use a test point not on the line. Which point is easiest?
steps.reveal: Use (0, 0) whenever the line does not pass through the origin. It makes substitution simple. Check: does y = 2x + 1 pass through (0,0)? 0 = 1 is false, so (0,0) is safe to use.

steps.prompt: Substitute (0, 0) into y > 2x + 1. What do we get?
steps.reveal: Replace x with 0 and y with 0: 0 > 2(0) + 1, which is 0 > 1.

steps.prompt: Is 0 > 1 true or false?
steps.reveal: FALSE. 0 is not greater than 1.

steps.prompt: The test point made the inequality FALSE. Which side do we shade?
steps.reveal: Shade the side that does NOT contain (0, 0), because (0,0) is not a solution. We always shade the side that makes the inequality TRUE — here that is the opposite side from the origin.

steps.prompt: State the rule so you do not shade the wrong side.
steps.reveal: Substitute the test point. TRUE -> shade the side WITH the point. FALSE -> shade the side WITHOUT the point. The biggest mistake is shading toward the test point even when it gave a false statement.

nodes.title: Scatter Plots & Trend Lines
nodes.objective: Construct scatter plots, describe association, and fit informal trend lines.

workedExamples.title: Describing association — and why a trend is not a cause

steps.prompt: A scatter plot has hours studied on the x-axis and test score on the y-axis. As you move right (more hours), the dots rise (higher scores). What kind of association is this?
steps.reveal: This is a POSITIVE association: as one variable increases, the other tends to increase, so the cloud of points slopes upward from lower-left to upper-right.

steps.prompt: How would we describe a scatter where the dots slope DOWNWARD (more of x goes with less of y), like daily temperature vs. heater hours?
steps.reveal: That is a NEGATIVE association: as x increases, y tends to decrease, so the points slope down from upper-left to lower-right. If the dots showed no clear up-or-down pattern at all, we'd say there is NO association.

steps.prompt: Back to study hours vs. score: the upward trend looks strong. A classmate says 'This proves that studying CAUSES higher scores.' Is that conclusion valid from the scatter alone?
steps.reveal: No. A strong trend only tells us the two variables are CORRELATED — they move together. It does NOT prove one causes the other. Something else (sleep, prior knowledge, motivation) could drive both.

steps.prompt: State the valid conclusion in careful words.
steps.reveal: The valid conclusion is: 'Hours studied and test score are positively correlated.' Claiming 'studying causes the higher score' is the causation-from-correlation error — correlation alone cannot establish cause.

steps.prompt: What is the takeaway rule for reading any scatter plot?
steps.reveal: Read the DIRECTION (positive, negative, or none) and the STRENGTH of the pattern, but never upgrade 'these move together' into 'this one causes that one.' Correlation does not imply causation.

workedExamples.title: Fitting an informal trend line — it need not pass through the origin

steps.prompt: A scatter shows a positive trend. The points cluster around the values: at x = 0 the data sits near y = 5, and the cloud rises by about 2 in y for every 1 in x. We want an informal trend line through the center of the data. What two things must a good trend line capture?
steps.reveal: A good informal trend line follows the CENTER of the data (about as many points above as below) and matches its overall STEEPNESS. Here the center starts near y = 5 and climbs about 2 per step.

steps.prompt: Where should this trend line cross the y-axis (its y-intercept)?
steps.reveal: At about y = 5, because that is where the data cloud sits when x = 0. The y-intercept should match the data — here it is clearly NOT zero.

steps.prompt: A classmate insists 'a trend line always has to start at (0, 0).' Is that correct?
steps.reveal: No. Forcing the line through the origin (0, 0) is the forces-line-through-origin error. A trend line only passes through (0,0) if the DATA actually sits near zero when x = 0. Here the data sits near 5, so the line should cross at about (0, 5).

steps.prompt: Write an informal trend line that fits this data.
steps.reveal: Using y-intercept about 5 and slope about 2: y = 2x + 5. This follows the center of the cloud and crosses the y-axis near 5 — not at the origin.

steps.prompt: How do we check the trend line is reasonable?
steps.reveal: Look that roughly half the points fall above the line and half below, and that the line's tilt matches the cloud's tilt. A line forced through (0,0) here (y = 2x) would sit too low and leave most points above it — a poor fit.

nodes.title: Arithmetic Sequences
nodes.objective: Identify common differences and write explicit rules for arithmetic sequences.

contextHooks.baseball: A card collection adds 6 cards a week: aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)·6, starting the count at week one's stack.
contextHooks.softball: Adding 2 mph of velocity per month follows a common difference.
contextHooks.basketball: Free-throw streaks rising 5 per week form a sequence.
contextHooks.soccer: Season tickets adding 3 matches a year: arithmetic growth.
contextHooks.football: Bench press up 5 pounds weekly — write the nth-week rule.
contextHooks.volleyball: Serve speed gains of 1 mph per week sequence cleanly.
contextHooks.neutral: aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d — a line sampled at whole numbers.

workedExamples.title: Finding the common difference by subtracting: 4, 7, 10, 13, …

steps.prompt: We have the sequence 4, 7, 10, 13. To find the common difference d, what operation connects each term to the next — adding or multiplying?
steps.reveal: Arithmetic sequences ADD the same amount each step. So we find d by SUBTRACTING a term from the one after it, not by dividing. This is the key trap: arithmetic means a constant difference, not a constant ratio.

steps.prompt: Subtract the first term from the second: 7 − 4. What do you get?
steps.reveal: 7 − 4 = 3. So one candidate for d is 3. But one gap is not enough — we must check that the SAME amount is added every time.

steps.prompt: Check the next gaps: 10 − 7 and 13 − 10. Do they match?
steps.reveal: 10 − 7 = 3 and 13 − 10 = 3. Every gap is 3, so the common difference is d = 3. The sequence truly adds 3 each step.

steps.prompt: Why is d = 3 (subtraction) correct, and what is the ratio trap?
steps.reveal: If you DIVIDED 7 ÷ 4 you would get 1.75, treating it like a geometric ratio — that is the wrong idea here. Arithmetic sequences are built by adding d = 3, found by subtraction. The common difference is 3.

workedExamples.title: Writing and using the explicit rule a_n = a_1 + (n − 1)d

steps.prompt: A sequence starts at a_1 = 5 with common difference d = 4: 5, 9, 13, … The explicit rule is a_n = a_1 + (n − 1)d. Substitute a_1 and d.
steps.reveal: a_n = 5 + (n − 1)·4. The (n − 1) is doing the work: it counts the number of GAPS, not the number of terms.

steps.prompt: To reach the 1st term, how many times do we add d? Test n = 1.
steps.reveal: a_1 = 5 + (1 − 1)·4 = 5 + 0 = 5. At the first term you have added d ZERO times. That is exactly why the formula uses (n − 1), not n.

steps.prompt: Now find the 10th term. How many differences of 4 do we add — 10 or 9?
steps.reveal: We add 9 differences, because (n − 1) = (10 − 1) = 9. To get from term 1 to term 10 you take 9 steps, not 10. Counting 10 steps is the classic off-by-one error.

steps.prompt: Compute a_10 and name the off-by-one trap value.
steps.reveal: a_10 = 5 + (10 − 1)·4 = 5 + 9·4 = 5 + 36 = 41. If you wrongly used n·d = 10·4 = 40 you'd get 5 + 40 = 45 — one extra difference. The correct 10th term is 41.

nodes.title: Direct Variation
nodes.objective: Recognize y = kx relationships and find constants of proportionality.

contextHooks.baseball: Total bases vary directly with hits when every hit's a single.
contextHooks.softball: Pitches thrown varies directly with batters faced at a steady rate.
contextHooks.basketball: Points from threes: p = 3t, straight through the origin.
contextHooks.soccer: Distance covered varies directly with minutes at constant pace.
contextHooks.football: Yards = 5.5 × carries when the rate never wavers.

workedExamples.title: Direct variation y = kx: find the constant k from a point

steps.prompt: A direct variation has the form y = kx. A pitcher throws a steady 15 pitches per inning, so pitches y vary directly with innings x. After 4 innings she has thrown 60 pitches, giving the point (4, 60). What does 'direct variation' mean about the graph?
steps.reveal: In direct variation y = kx, there is NO added number. The graph is a straight line through the ORIGIN (0, 0): zero innings means zero pitches. There is no '+ b' term sitting on top.

steps.prompt: To find the constant of variation k, what do we do with the point (4, 60)?
steps.reveal: Use k = y/x. Divide the y-value by the x-value: k = 60 / 4. We are NOT subtracting anything first — there is no b to remove, because direct variation has no constant added.

steps.prompt: Compute k = 60 / 4.
steps.reveal: k = 15. So the equation is y = 15x. The common trap is to act as if y = kx + b and 'solve' for a smaller slope by subtracting a made-up constant — but a direct variation has no b, so k is simply y/x.

steps.prompt: Check k by testing the origin and the point.
steps.reveal: At x = 0: y = 15(0) = 0, so the line passes through (0, 0) as required. At x = 4: y = 15(4) = 60, matching the point. The constant of variation is k = 15.

steps.prompt: What is the one-sentence takeaway?
steps.reveal: For direct variation y = kx, find k by dividing y by x from any point, and remember the graph always runs through the origin with no constant added.

workedExamples.title: Direct variation vs. y = kx + b: k is the constant of variation, NOT a y-intercept

steps.prompt: Two rules are compared. Rule A: y = 6x. Rule B: y = 6x + 5. Only one is a direct variation. Which one, and why?
steps.reveal: Rule A (y = 6x) is the direct variation: it has the form y = kx with no added constant. Rule B (y = 6x + 5) has a constant +5, so it is NOT a direct variation — the +5 shifts the line off the origin.

steps.prompt: Test each rule at x = 0.
steps.reveal: Rule A: y = 6(0) = 0, so it passes through (0, 0). Rule B: y = 6(0) + 5 = 5, so it passes through (0, 5), NOT the origin. A direct variation MUST pass through the origin; Rule B fails this test.

steps.prompt: In Rule A, y = 6x, what number is the constant of variation k?
steps.reveal: k = 6. This is the slope of the line — how fast y grows per unit of x. It is NOT a y-intercept. The y-intercept of y = 6x is 0.

steps.prompt: In Rule B, y = 6x + 5, a student says 'k = 5 because 5 is the constant.' Why is that wrong?
steps.reveal: The 5 is a y-intercept (the constant added), not the constant of variation. Rule B is not even a direct variation. Confusing the added constant for k is the classic 'k-as-y-intercept' error: k is the multiplier on x (the slope), never the number added on.

steps.prompt: State the rule that separates the two forms.
steps.reveal: y = kx is direct variation: passes through the origin, k is the slope/constant of variation. y = kx + b (b ≠ 0) is NOT direct variation: the constant b is a y-intercept, and k is still the slope — never read the y-intercept as k.

nodes.title: Systems by Graphing
nodes.objective: Solve a system of linear equations as the intersection point of two lines.

contextHooks.baseball: Two hitters' pace lines cross at the game their totals tie.
contextHooks.softball: Strikeout paces intersect — read the meeting point.
contextHooks.basketball: Your scoring line catches the leader's where they cross.
contextHooks.soccer: Two clubs' points lines intersect at the table-flip match.
contextHooks.football: Rushing pace lines cross at the week the race ties.
contextHooks.volleyball: Kill paces meet at one set — the intersection.
contextHooks.neutral: The solution is the one point both lines share.

workedExamples.title: Graph both lines and read the intersection as an ordered pair

steps.prompt: We want to solve the system y = x + 1 and y = -x + 5 by graphing. First graph y = x + 1. What is its y-intercept and slope?
steps.reveal: y-intercept b = 1, so start at the point (0, 1). Slope m = 1, so go up 1 and right 1 to reach (1, 2), then (2, 3), and so on. Draw the line through those points.

steps.prompt: Now graph y = -x + 5 on the same grid. What is its y-intercept and slope?
steps.reveal: y-intercept b = 5, so start at (0, 5). Slope m = -1, so go down 1 and right 1 to reach (1, 4), then (2, 3), and so on. Draw this line through those points.

steps.prompt: The solution of the system is the point where the two lines cross. Find the grid point both lines pass through.
steps.reveal: Both lines pass through (2, 3): on the first line, going (0,1)->(1,2)->(2,3); on the second, going (0,5)->(1,4)->(2,3). They cross at (2, 3).

steps.prompt: Read the intersection carefully. What is the x-coordinate, and what is the y-coordinate?
steps.reveal: The x-coordinate is 2 and the y-coordinate is 3. Read BOTH numbers off the axes — an intersection is one ordered pair (x, y), not a single number. Sliding one square off would give a wrong answer like (2, 4) or (3, 3).

steps.prompt: Write the solution of the system as an ordered pair.
steps.reveal: The solution is (2, 3). Type it as (x, y), x first then y, separated by a comma.

workedExamples.title: Check a candidate intersection by substituting into BOTH equations

steps.prompt: A student graphs y = 2x - 1 and y = x + 1 and claims the lines cross at (2, 3). To check, substitute x = 2, y = 3 into the FIRST equation y = 2x - 1. Does it hold?
steps.reveal: Right side: 2(2) - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3. Left side y = 3. So 3 = 3 is true. The point (2, 3) lies on the first line.

steps.prompt: Now substitute the same point x = 2, y = 3 into the SECOND equation y = x + 1. Does it hold?
steps.reveal: Right side: 2 + 1 = 3. Left side y = 3. So 3 = 3 is true. The point (2, 3) also lies on the second line.

steps.prompt: Why does passing BOTH checks mean (2, 3) is the solution of the system?
steps.reveal: The solution must lie on both lines at once — that is exactly what the intersection is. Since (2, 3) satisfies both equations, it is the one point the two lines share.

steps.prompt: Suppose instead the check gave 3 = 3 for the first equation but 3 = 4 for the second. What would that tell you?
steps.reveal: The point is on the first line but NOT the second, so it is not the intersection. A failed check means a line was graphed wrong — recheck the slope and y-intercept of the line that failed and find where the lines really cross.

steps.prompt: State the verified solution of the system.
steps.reveal: The solution is (2, 3), confirmed because it satisfies both equations. Always substitute the candidate point into BOTH equations before trusting it.

p1.prompt: Two hitters' season home-run totals are modeled by y = x + 2 and y = 2x, where x is months into the season. Graph both lines and find the point where their totals are equal — the intersection (type as (x, y)).

The intersection is the one grid point both lines pass through; read both coordinates.

nodes.title: Systems by Substitution
nodes.objective: Solve systems algebraically by substituting one expression into the other equation.

contextHooks.baseball: y = 2x doubles-to-singles ratio inside x + y = 9 hits.
contextHooks.softball: Express walks via strikeouts, substitute into the total.
contextHooks.basketball: y = 2x threes-to-twos relation inside the points total.
contextHooks.soccer: Assists defined by goals, substituted into involvements.
contextHooks.football: Pass yards as a function of rush yards inside total offense.
contextHooks.volleyball: Blocks expressed through kills inside the points equation.
contextHooks.neutral: Replace a variable with its equal expression; solve one unknown.

workedExamples.title: Substitute into the OTHER equation: y = x + 2 and 3x + y = 10

steps.prompt: You have y = x + 2 and 3x + y = 10. The first equation already tells you what y equals. Which equation should the expression x + 2 go INTO?
steps.reveal: Put x + 2 into the OTHER equation, 3x + y = 10. If you substitute x + 2 back into y = x + 2 (its own source), you get x + 2 = x + 2 — always true, but it tells you nothing. Substitution only makes progress in the equation it did not come from.

steps.prompt: Replace y with x + 2 in 3x + y = 10. Write the new equation.
steps.reveal: 3x + (x + 2) = 10. Now there is only one variable, x, so the equation can actually be solved.

steps.prompt: Combine like terms and solve for x.
steps.reveal: 3x + x + 2 = 10, so 4x + 2 = 10. Subtract 2: 4x = 8. Divide by 4: x = 2.

steps.prompt: You found x = 2. Are you finished?
steps.reveal: Not yet — a system asks for BOTH unknowns. Back-substitute x = 2 into the simplest equation, y = x + 2: y = 2 + 2 = 4.

steps.prompt: State the full solution and check it.
steps.reveal: The solution is (2, 4). Check both: y = x + 2 gives 4 = 2 + 2 (true), and 3x + y = 10 gives 3(2) + 4 = 6 + 4 = 10 (true). Both equations hold, so (2, 4) is correct.

workedExamples.title: Don't stop at x: back-substitute to finish (x = 2y − 1 and x + y = 8)

steps.prompt: You have x = 2y − 1 and x + y = 8. One equation is already solved for x. Substitute 2y − 1 into the OTHER equation.
steps.reveal: Replace x in x + y = 8: (2y − 1) + y = 8. Substituting into x = 2y − 1 itself would only give 2y − 1 = 2y − 1, a useless identity.

steps.prompt: Solve (2y − 1) + y = 8 for y.
steps.reveal: Combine: 3y − 1 = 8. Add 1: 3y = 9. Divide by 3: y = 3.

steps.prompt: You found y = 3. A common mistake is to report '3' and stop. Why is that not the answer?
steps.reveal: The solution to a two-variable system is an ordered pair (x, y) — a single point. You have only one coordinate so far. You still need x.

steps.prompt: Back-substitute y = 3 to find x.
Write the ordered pair and verify it in both equations.
steps.reveal: The solution is (5, 3). Check: x = 2y − 1 gives 5 = 2(3) − 1 = 5 (true); x + y = 8 gives 5 + 3 = 8 (true). Report the full pair (5, 3), never just one number.

nodes.objective: Solve systems by adding or subtracting scaled equations to eliminate a variable.

workedExamples.title: Scale one equation, then eliminate: 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 4y = 12

steps.prompt: We want to eliminate y from 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 4y = 12. The y-coefficients are 2 and −4. If you just ADD the equations as they are, what happens to y?
steps.reveal: You get 2y + (−4y) = −2y. Nothing fully cancels, because 2 and 4 are different sizes. Adding without scaling leaves a y term. You must first make the coefficients match in size.

steps.prompt: Multiply the FIRST equation by 2 so its y-coefficient becomes 4. What does it become?
steps.reveal: 2 × (3x + 2y = 16) gives 6x + 4y = 32. Multiply EVERY term by 2: 2·3x = 6x, 2·2y = 4y, 2·16 = 32. Now the y-coefficients are +4 and −4.

steps.prompt: Add 6x + 4y = 32 to 5x − 4y = 12. What equation in x do you get?
Substitute x = 4 into 3x + 2y = 16 to find y.
Check (4, 2) in BOTH original equations.

workedExamples.title: Subtract equations, distributing the minus to every term: 4x + 3y = 20 and 4x + y = 12

steps.prompt: In 4x + 3y = 20 and 4x + y = 12, both x-coefficients are 4. To eliminate x, do you add or subtract?
steps.reveal: Subtract. When matching coefficients have the SAME sign (both +4), subtracting cancels x. Adding would give 8x and cancel nothing.

steps.prompt: Subtracting the second equation means subtracting EVERY term of it. Write (4x + 3y) − (4x + y) and 20 − 12.
steps.reveal: The minus distributes to all of the second equation: −(4x + y) = −4x − y. So the left side is 4x + 3y − 4x − y. The classic error is writing 4x + 3y − 4x + y — forgetting to flip the +y to −y.

steps.prompt: Combine like terms on the left, and subtract on the right.
Substitute y = 4 into 4x + y = 12, then check both equations.

nodes.title: Systems: Special Cases
nodes.objective: Recognize systems with no solution or infinitely many solutions.

contextHooks.baseball: Identical paces from different starts never tie — no solution.
contextHooks.softball: Same line written two ways: infinitely many shared points.
contextHooks.basketball: Parallel scoring lines mean the gap never closes.
contextHooks.soccer: Equivalent points equations describe one identical line.
contextHooks.football: Same rate, different head start: the chase never ends.
contextHooks.volleyball: Two descriptions of one kill pace — every point works.
contextHooks.neutral: 0 = 5 → no solution. 0 = 0 → infinitely many.

workedExamples.title: Collapsing to 0 = 0: the same line, infinitely many solutions

steps.prompt: Solve the system y = 2x + 1 and 2y = 4x + 2. Both equations have a y. Solve the second one for y to compare them.
steps.reveal: Divide every term of 2y = 4x + 2 by 2: y = 2x + 1. The second equation is exactly the first equation in disguise.

steps.prompt: Both equations are now y = 2x + 1. Use substitution: replace y in the first with 2x + 1 from the second.
steps.reveal: (2x + 1) = 2x + 1. Subtract 2x from both sides, then subtract 1 from both sides: 0 = 0.

steps.prompt: You got 0 = 0. Is that a true statement or a false statement?
steps.reveal: 0 = 0 is TRUE — it is true for every value of x. That is the signal that the two equations describe the very same line.

steps.prompt: What does one single line for both equations mean about where they cross?
steps.reveal: The two lines lie perfectly on top of each other, so they share EVERY point. There are infinitely many solutions.

steps.prompt: Watch the trap: a student sees 0 = 0 and writes 'no solution.' Why is that wrong?
steps.reveal: 0 = 0 is true, not impossible. A TRUE collapse means infinitely many solutions. 'No solution' only happens when the collapse is FALSE, like 0 = 5. Same slope AND same intercept (here slope 2, intercept 1 for both) confirms infinitely many.

workedExamples.title: Parallel lines: same slope, different intercept, no solution

steps.prompt: Solve the system y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x + 4. Compare the slopes of the two lines first.
steps.reveal: Both slopes are 3. Equal slopes mean the lines rise at the same rate, so they are parallel — unless they are the exact same line.

steps.prompt: Now compare the y-intercepts to tell 'parallel' from 'same line.'
steps.reveal: The first crosses the y-axis at 1, the second at 4. Same slope but DIFFERENT intercepts means two distinct parallel lines.

steps.prompt: Use substitution to confirm: set the two expressions for y equal.
steps.reveal: 3x + 1 = 3x + 4. Subtract 3x from both sides: 1 = 4.

steps.prompt: You got 1 = 4. Is that true or false, and what does it mean?
steps.reveal: 1 = 4 is FALSE — it can never be true. A false collapse means the lines never meet: NO solution.

steps.prompt: Watch the trap: a student says parallel lines have 'one solution.' Why is that wrong?
steps.reveal: Parallel lines run side by side forever and NEVER cross, so there is no point in common — no solution. One solution requires the lines to cross exactly once, which needs DIFFERENT slopes.

nodes.title: Systems Word Problems
nodes.objective: Model two-constraint situations as systems, solve, and interpret in context.

contextHooks.baseball: Tickets and concessions: two totals, two unknowns, one system.
contextHooks.softball: Bats and gloves bought under a count and a budget constraint.
contextHooks.basketball: Twos and threes from total makes and total points.
contextHooks.soccer: Wins and draws recovered from matches played and points earned.
contextHooks.football: TDs and field goals from scores and scoring plays.
contextHooks.volleyball: Kills and aces from total points and total attempts.
contextHooks.neutral: Two facts about two unknowns — define both, build both equations.

workedExamples.title: Two constraints need two equations

steps.prompt: A school fair sells adult and child tickets. Two facts are given: 9 tickets were sold in all, AND the money collected was $51. Before writing any equations, what must you do first?
steps.reveal: Define your variables clearly. Let a = the number of adult tickets and c = the number of child tickets. Naming the unknowns prevents the most common error: not knowing which number answers the question at the end.

steps.prompt: The first constraint is 'a total of 9 tickets were sold.' Write that as an equation.
steps.reveal: a + c = 9. This single equation counts tickets. By itself it cannot tell you how many of each — many (a, c) pairs add to 9, so one equation is not enough.

steps.prompt: The second constraint is 'the money collected was $51.' Adult tickets cost $7 and child tickets cost $4. Write that as an equation.
steps.reveal: 7a + 4c = 51. This equation tracks dollars, a completely different fact from the ticket count.

steps.prompt: Why can't you answer the question with just one of these equations?
steps.reveal: Each equation captures only ONE constraint. Two unknowns pinned down by two separate facts require TWO equations solved together. Using one equation alone is the classic single-equation-for-two-constraints mistake.

steps.prompt: State the finished system.
steps.reveal: a + c = 9 and 7a + 4c = 51, with a = adult tickets and c = child tickets. Two constraints, two labeled variables, two equations — ready to solve.

workedExamples.title: Solve the system and interpret the answer

steps.prompt: Solve the system from before: a + c = 9 and 7a + 4c = 51. Start by isolating one variable from the simpler equation.
steps.reveal: From a + c = 9, write c = 9 − a. Substitution replaces c in the other equation with an expression in a.

steps.prompt: Substitute c = 9 − a into 7a + 4c = 51 and simplify.
Solve for a, then find c.
Check (a, c) = (5, 4) against BOTH original constraints.
steps.reveal: Tickets: 5 + 4 = 9 ✓. Money: 7(5) + 4(4) = 35 + 16 = 51 ✓. A solution must satisfy both facts, not just one.

steps.prompt: Interpret the answer in context with the right labels.
steps.reveal: 5 adult tickets and 4 child tickets were sold. Always restate which count is which — the bare numbers 5 and 4 mean nothing until you attach 'adult' and 'child.'

p1.prompt: At a game, adult tickets are $8 and child tickets are $5. A family bought 6 tickets in all and spent $39. Let a = number of adult tickets and c = number of child tickets, so a + c = 6 and 8a + 5c = 39. How many ADULT tickets did they buy? Type a number only.
hints: Two facts (6 tickets, $39 spent) need both equations solved together, not just one.
From a + c = 6, write c = 6 − a, then substitute into 8a + 5c = 39.

p1.prompt: A hitter's at-bats were all singles or doubles. He had 10 hits in all that produced 13 total bases (a single = 1 base, a double = 2 bases). Let s = number of singles and d = number of doubles, so s + d = 10 and s + 2d = 13. How many DOUBLES did he hit? Type a number only.
hints: The hit count and the base count are two different constraints; use both equations.
Subtract s + d = 10 from s + 2d = 13 to get d directly.

p1.prompt: A pitcher threw 12 strikeouts and walks combined, and the strikeouts were 4 more than the walks. Let k = number of strikeouts and w = number of walks, so k + w = 12 and k = w + 4. Give your answer as (k, w) = (strikeouts, walks). Type as (x, y).
hints: Substitute k = w + 4 into k + w = 12 and solve for w first.
Order matters: the first number is strikeouts (k), the second is walks (w).

p1.prompt: A team sold programs at the gate. Single programs cost $3 and combo programs cost $5. They sold p single programs and q combo programs, with p + q = 20 programs sold for $76 total. Which system models this situation? Let p = single programs and q = combo programs.
hints: You need one equation for the count (20 programs) and one for the dollars ($76).
Each price multiplies its OWN program type: $3 goes with singles p, $5 with combos q.

p1.prompt: A coach bought softballs at $4 each and gloves at $9 each, 7 items in all, spending $43. Let b = number of softballs and g = number of gloves, so b + g = 7 and 4b + 9g = 43. How many GLOVES were bought? Type a number only.
hints: The item count and the budget are two constraints; solve both equations together.
From b + g = 7, write b = 7 − g, then substitute into 4b + 9g = 43.

p1.prompt: A batter had 11 hits that were singles or triples, totaling 19 bases (a single = 1 base, a triple = 3 bases). Let s = number of singles and t = number of triples, so s + t = 11 and s + 3t = 19. How many TRIPLES were hit? Type a number only.
hints: Hit count and base count are separate facts; use both equations.
Subtract s + t = 11 from s + 3t = 19 to isolate t.

p1.prompt: A pitcher recorded 15 outs by strikeout or groundout, and the strikeouts were twice the groundouts. Let k = number of strikeouts and r = number of groundouts, so k + r = 15 and k = 2r. Give your answer as (k, r) = (strikeouts, groundouts). Type as (x, y).
hints: Substitute k = 2r into k + r = 15 and solve for r first.
Order matters: first number is strikeouts (k), second is groundouts (r).

p1.prompt: A booster table sold wristbands at $2 and pennants at $6. They sold w wristbands and n pennants, with w + n = 18 items sold for $68 total. Which system models this situation? Let w = wristbands and n = pennants.
hints: One equation for the item count (18) and one for the dollars ($68).
Each price multiplies its own item: $2 with wristbands w, $6 with pennants n.

p1.prompt: A player scored only on two-point and three-point shots. She made 11 shots in all for 25 points. Let x = number of two-point shots and y = number of three-point shots, so x + y = 11 and 2x + 3y = 25. How many THREE-POINT shots did she make? Type a number only.
hints: The shot count and the point total are two constraints; solve both together.
From x + y = 11, write x = 11 − y, then substitute into 2x + 3y = 25.

p1.prompt: A guard scored on free throws (1 point) and two-point baskets, making 14 scoring plays for 22 points. Let f = number of free throws and b = number of two-point baskets, so f + b = 14 and f + 2b = 22. How many TWO-POINT baskets did he make? Type a number only.
hints: Scoring-play count and point total are separate facts; use both equations.
Subtract f + b = 14 from f + 2b = 22 to isolate b.

p1.prompt: A team grabbed 16 rebounds, offensive or defensive, and the defensive rebounds were 3 times the offensive rebounds. Let o = offensive rebounds and d = defensive rebounds, so o + d = 16 and d = 3o. Give your answer as (o, d) = (offensive, defensive). Type as (x, y).
hints: Substitute d = 3o into o + d = 16 and solve for o first.
Order matters: first number is offensive (o), second is defensive (d).

Substitute n = f + 5 into n + f = 13 and solve for f, then find n.

p1.prompt: A booster table sold posters at $3 and shirts at $9. They sold p posters and r shirts, with p + r = 13 items sold for $87 total. Which system models this situation? Let p = posters and r = shirts.

p1.prompt: A store sold 10 drinks, small or large, for $26 (a small = $2, a large = $3). Let s = number of smalls and l = number of larges, so s + l = 10 and 2s + 3l = 26. How many LARGE drinks were sold? Type a number only.

workedExamples.title: Feasible region of a system is the OVERLAP (intersection), not the union

steps.prompt: A system has two inequalities: y ≥ x and y ≤ 4. We shade each one. What region answers the SYSTEM?
steps.reveal: A solution of the SYSTEM must make BOTH inequalities true at the same time. The answer is the OVERLAP — the region where the shading from y ≥ x and the shading from y ≤ 4 cover the SAME points. Where only one is shaded is not a solution.

steps.prompt: A student shades everything that satisfies y ≥ x OR y ≤ 4 and calls it the answer. Why is that wrong?
steps.reveal: That is the UNION (either-or), which is far too big. A system requires AND, not OR. The union counts points that satisfy only one inequality; those points fail the system. We keep only the intersection (the doubly-shaded slice).

steps.prompt: Test the point (1, 3). Is it in the feasible region?
steps.reveal: Check BOTH: y ≥ x → 3 ≥ 1 true. y ≤ 4 → 3 ≤ 4 true. Both hold, so (1, 3) is in the overlap and IS a solution of the system.

steps.prompt: Test the point (5, 3). Is it a solution?
steps.reveal: Check BOTH: y ≥ x → 3 ≥ 5 FALSE. y ≤ 4 → 3 ≤ 4 true. It satisfies only ONE inequality, so it is in the union but NOT in the overlap. It is NOT a solution of the system.

steps.prompt: State the rule in one sentence.
steps.reveal: The feasible region of a system of inequalities is the intersection — the overlap where ALL inequalities are satisfied at once; a point counts only if it passes every inequality, never just one.

workedExamples.title: Each boundary keeps its OWN style: dashed for strict < or >, solid for ≤ or ≥

steps.prompt: A system is y > 2x − 1 and y ≤ x + 3. Both lines get drawn. Do both boundaries look the same?
steps.reveal: No. Each boundary is styled by its OWN inequality sign. y > 2x − 1 uses a STRICT sign (>), so that boundary is DASHED. y ≤ x + 3 uses ≤ (allows equal), so that boundary is SOLID. A single system can mix one dashed and one solid line.

steps.prompt: Why is the boundary of y > 2x − 1 dashed?
steps.reveal: Strict inequalities (< or >) do NOT include the line itself — points exactly on the line make it 'equal,' which '>' forbids. We draw the line dashed to show those boundary points are excluded.

steps.prompt: Why is the boundary of y ≤ x + 3 solid?
steps.reveal: ≤ and ≥ INCLUDE equality, so points exactly on the line ARE solutions. We draw the line solid to show the boundary itself is part of the region.

steps.prompt: A student draws BOTH boundaries solid because it is one system. What is the error?
steps.reveal: Boundary style is per-inequality, not per-system. Matching both to the same style is a boundary-type mismatch. You must read each sign separately: > stays dashed, ≤ stays solid — even within the same system.

steps.prompt: State the rule in one sentence.
steps.reveal: Match each boundary to its own inequality: dashed for strict < or >, solid for ≤ or ≥ — so a system can legitimately show a mix of solid and dashed lines.
